topic_info.title: Purulent skin and soft tissue infections (furuncle, carbuncle, abscess)

list.listitem: Purulent skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) present as furuncles (boils), carbuncles (interconnected boils), and abscesses. C
When clinical exam is uncertain, perform point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) to rule out the presence of abscess. A
Whenever possible, treat purulent SSTIs using incision and drainage (I&D). B
Consider obtaining a wound culture when performing I&D. C

In communities with high prevalence (>45%) of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) among abscess isolates, consider adding MRSA coverage (eg, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole [TMP/SMX]) after I&D to improve cure rates for abscesses 2 to 5 cm in adults and children (NNT 7 to 14), but monitor the patient for mild gastrointestinal adverse events like diarrhea (NNH 10 to 15). A
Consider systemic antibiotics in addition to I&D for purulent SSTIs that involve multiple lesions, surrounding cellulitis, gangrene, immunocompromised hosts, or systemic signs of infection. C

background.definition: A furuncle (boil) is a deep infection of the hair follicle that is walled off, enclosing a collection of pus. A carbuncle is a painful, deep, interconnected aggregate of abscessed hair follicles (furuncles). An abscess is a collection of pus or purulent material within the dermis and deeper layers of the skin and soft tissue, clinically presenting as a warm, erythematous, tender, edematous, fluctuant subcutaneous cyst or nodule.

list.listitem: Annual incidence has ranged from 18.0 to 25.7/100,000 cases of CA-MRSA, 77% of which are SSTIs, based on population and hospital-laboratory surveillance in three US cities.
Invasive disease (bacteremia, sepsis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, endocarditis) may occur with CA-MRSA but is relatively uncommon compared to health care associated MRSA.
Staphylococcus aureus is the usual cause, more than 59% skin abscesses present with CA-MRSA.
Gram negative bacteria (Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) are relatively rare.
Anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Peptococcus, Lactobacillus species) may contribute to the polymicrobial nature of a skin abscess.
Infection of the hair follicle, usually by S. aureus, leads to suppuration through the dermis into the subcutaneous tissue where a collection of pus (abscess) forms.
Infection is primarily spread by direct skin-to-skin contact, typically via hands.

CA-MRSA is genetically distinct from hospital-acquired MRSA, containing staphylococcal cassette chromosome (SCC) mec type IV, which is multidrug resistant and frequently has a dermonecrotic exotoxin (Panton-Valentine leukocidin) that contributes to formation of skin abscesses.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Any antibiotic taken in past month
Men who have sex with men
Patient contact in health care setting
Recent hospitalization or surgery (withing past 2 months)

list.listitem: For patients with recurrent S. aureus infections, consider daily decontamination of clothes, towels, and sheets. C

Among patients discharged from the hospital who are MRSA-colonized, education plus intensive postdischarge decolonization involving 4% chlorhexidine baths or showers once daily, 0.12% chlorhexidine mouthwash twice daily, and 2% nasal mupirocin twice daily for 5 days twice per month for 6 months decreases subsequent MRSA infections (NNT 30), infections from any cause, and MRSA-associated hospitalizations at one year (NNT 34), compared to education alone. B

Among healthy soldiers nasally colonized with CA-MRSA, eradication therapy using nasal mupirocin did not decrease the incidence of MRSA infection nor prevent new MRSA colonization, compared with placebo. B
Purulent skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) present as furuncles (boils), carbuncles (interconnected boils), and abscesses. C
Consider furuncle or carbuncle (especially CA-MRSA) in the differential for patients who present with a "spider bite." C
When clinical exam is uncertain, perform point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) to rule out the presence of abscess. A
Consider obtaining a wound culture when performing I&D. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Identified by overlying skin pore opening, preexisting nodule, or mass
Groin and inguinal locations, usually recurrent
Face and upper torso sites, with acne scarring
Often multiple, located on anterior lower legs
More superficial and widespread, not pustular, and often on lower extremities

list.listitem: Purulent SSTIs are painful lesions in the absence of trauma that are cystic or nodular, solitary, warm, and erythematous; patient might attribute it to an insect or spider bite.

Lesion may present as a tender nodule with visible pustule, warm firm plaque, or fluctuant cyst. Less common associated findings may include cellulitis, impetigo (honey-colored crust), or infected wound.
Look for skin injection sites among intravenous drug users.
Ask about risk factors for MRSA (see ).
Obtain a wound culture during I&D.

POCUS may improve diagnostic accuracy of SSTIs in children when clinical examination alone is inconclusive. Sensitivity of the clinical examination is 44%, which improves to 78% when POCUS is performed.

POCUS in an emergency room or outpatient setting can be helpful in ruling out abscesses when differentiating between abscess vs cellulitis. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 RCTs involving 2656 patients showed POCUS to be 94.6% sensitive and 85.4% specific in diagnosing an abscess (LR+ 6.5, LR- 0.06).

A prospective study of 1216 patients found that in cases where there is clinical uncertainty regarding the presence or absence of abscess, performing POCUS lead to a change in the decision to perform I&D in 23% of cases, and that this decision change was appropriate in 84% of these cases.
See . Collect specimen of pus for bacterial culture when performing I&D.
I&D is of paramount importance in treatment of abscess and should be done whenever possible.
Consider nasal swab for bacterial culture to evaluate for colonization in patients with multiple or recurrent SSTIs.
Whenever possible, treat purulent SSTIs using I&D. B

In communities with a high prevalence (>45%) of CA-MRSA among abscess isolates, consider adding MRSA coverage (eg, TMP/SMX) after I&D to improve cure rates for abscesses 2 to 5 cm in adults and children (NNT 7 to 14). Monitor the patient for mild gastrointestinal adverse events like diarrhea (NNH 10 to 15). A
Consider systemic antibiotics in addition to I&D for purulent SSTIs that involve multiple lesions, surrounding cellulitis, gangrene, immunocompromised hosts, or systemic signs of infection. C
See for an outline of the general approach. Risk factors for MRSA are outlined in .

For simple cutaneous abscesses, older data found no strong evidence for the routine use of antibiotics after I&D. Two studies showed no differences in outcome for CA-MRSA SSTIs that were treated with active (ie, cultures showing sensitivity to that antibiotic) instead of inactive antibiotics.

However, more contemporary studies in communities with high prevalence (>45%) of CA-MRSA among abscess isolates have shown better cure rates when MRSA coverage (7-10 days) is added (eg, TMP/SMX, clindamycin) after I&D of abscesses 2 to 5 cm in adults and children (NNT 7 to 14). However, there were higher rates of mild gastrointestinal adverse events like diarrhea among patients treated with antibiotics (NNH 10 to 15).

Subsequently, a systematic review and meta-analysis of 4 studies including 2406 patients found an increased rate of clinical cure with antibiotic treatment after I&D as compared to placebo. Similarly, a second systematic review of 14 trials involving 3541 patients concluded treating with clindamycin or TMP/SMX results in improved outcomes after I&D. These authors cautioned against potential adverse effects seen with antibiotic usage, which are mostly mild and self-limited.

2014 IDSA guidelines recommend considering antibiotics in purulent SSTIs that involve multiple lesions, gangrene, immunocompromised patients, surrounding cellulitis, or systemic signs of infection (eg, fever). It is reasonable to treat for CA-MRSA if risk factors are present (see ) and to change to appropriate antibiotics once culture sensitivities return.

A Cochrane review in 2021 found no RCTs to evaluate the efficacy and safety of topical antibiotics compared to antiseptics, topical antibiotics compared to systemitc antibiotics, or phototherapy compared to sham light therapy for the treatment of furuncles and carbuncles.

According to the 2014 IDSA guidelines, for purulent SSTIs of moderate severity (ie, associated with systemic signs of infection), perform I&D and initiate empiric treatment using oral antibiotics with MRSA coverage such as trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), doxycycline, or clindamycin (if clindamycin resistance is <10-15% at the institution).
For purulent SSTIs of moderate severity and culture-confirmed methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA), use oral dicloxacillin or cephalexin.

In a randomized trial a computerized physician order entry (CPOE) system gave prompts that recommended standard-spectrum instead of extended-spectrum antibiotics during the first 72 hours for noncritically ill patients with skin and soft tissue infections who had less than 10% risk of Pseudomonas or multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) as assessed by an electronic health record model. CPOE prompts combined with provider education and feedback led to the reduced use of empiric extended-spectrum antibiotics for patients hospitalized with skin and soft tissue infections who have low risk for Pseudomonas or MDROs (RR 0.72 for use of broad spectrum antibiotic, 28% reduction).

Rifampin may be combined with tetracyclines or TMP/SMX for recurrent infections, but rifampin should never be used alone due to rapid emergence of resistance. Duration of treatment is typically 10 days.

For severe purulent SSTIs (ie, patients who have failed I&D plus oral antibiotics, fever >38 C, pulse >90, respirations >24 per minute, WBC <400 or >12,000, immunocompromised status), perform I&D, obtain cultures of abscess and blood, and initiate empiric therapy for MRSA using IV vancomycin (preferred) or IV daptomycin, linezolid, televancin, or ceftaroline.
For severe purulent SSTIs with culture-confirmed MSSA, stop IV vancomycin and switch to IV nafcillin, oxacillin, cefazolin, or clindamycin.

One randomized, open-label trial found linezolid at 600 mg IV or PO every 12 hours had equivalent cure rates in hospitalized complicated SSTIs, compared to vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours, and superior outcomes in the subset with MRSA infections, 89% versus 67% (p < 0.001).

A Cochrane review in 2016, based on evidence deemed at high risk of bias and studies entirely from the pharmaceutical maker of linezolid, found linezolid more effective than vancomycin for the treatment of SSTIs, including MRSA-associated SSTIs.
Daptomycin IV at 4 mg/kg every 24 hours for at least 3 days had similar success rates in complicated skin infections compared to vancomycin in an open-label trial.

IV dalbavancin is an alternative to IV vancomycin (followed by oral linezolid) for the treatment of severe acute bacterial skin infections (ie, cellulitis, abscess, or wound infection) as demonstrated in a randomized controlled trial. IV dalbavancin was dosed 1000 mg on day 1 and 500 mg on day 8 (ie, 2 doses only) and was assocaited with similar cure rates and lower mortality (0.2% vs 1.1%, p = 0.03) compared to IV vancomycin twice daily for 3 days followed by oral linezolid twice daily for 10 to 14 days of total antibiotic therapy.

A single dose of IV oritavancin appears non-inferior to IV vancomycin for 7 to 10 days for the treatment of severe acute gram-positive bacterial skin infections (ie, cellulitis, erysipelas, or large abscess of at least 75 cm2 of induration, erythema or edema).

A manufacturer sponsored study of 666 patients randomized to once daily IV tedizolid 200 mg for 6 days or twice daily linezolid for 10 days found no difference in clinical response (85% vs 83%). Patients could be stepped down to oral therapy if clinically stable.

Another manufacturer sponsored study of 861 patients randomized to omadacycline (450 mg PO daily for days 1-2, then 300 mg PO daily) or twice-daily linezolid 600 mg PO found that omadacycline was non-inferior to linezolid for treating major abscesses.
Other antibiotic options for severe acute bacterial SSTIs include delafloxacin (IV or PO for 5 to 14 days) and omadacycline (IV or PO for 7 to 14 days).
I&D, with breaking of loculations, is the primary treatment of large furuncles, carbuncles, and abscesses.
I&D with or without packing appear to have similar outcomes.

For infants and children up to 18 years of age, use of topical anesthetic cream (eg, lidocaine) under occlusion, prior to I&D, results to spontaneous drainage of abscess in a quarter of patients and decreases the use of procedural sedation.

Based on a meta-analysis of 8 studies involving 910 patients, conventional I&D appears more likely than the newer loop drainage technique (LDT) to lead to treatment failure of abscesses (OR 2.02, 95% CI 1.29-3.18). LDT entails creating two small incisions at opposite poles of the abscess, using small forceps to break loculations through these two incisions, then inserting a "vessel loop" and tying it over the skin surface to facilitate continued drainage, thereby avoiding the need for packing and minimizing postoperative visits. Some silicone vessel loops do not even require tying or suturing.
Post-I&D irrigation (with saline) does not appear to improve clinical outcomes compared to no irrigation.
Conflicting data exist on primary suture of incision versus leaving the wound open, although a systematic review recommended against primary closure.
Simple dry dressing may be the easiest dressing to apply after I&D.
Local or regional anesthesia may be needed if abscess is quite deep or large.
I&D with the assistance of POCUS resulted in less clinical failure than those performed without POCUS in an RCT of 125 patients.

Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is not an adequate treatment of superficial cutaneous abscesses. An RCT of 101 patients with superficial skin abscess compared ultrasound-guided aspiration with surgical I&D. There were more treatment failures with ultrasound-guided aspiration (74% vs 20%).
For small furuncles in uncomplicated patients, using moist heat packs which promote drainage may be considered as initial intervention prior to performing I&D.

Tap water may be similar to sterile water or saline when cleansing wounds. Boiled (then cooled) water and distilled water are other options. However, no strong evidence supports wound cleansing as an effective method to hasten wound healing or to decrease wound infections.
Systemic symptoms of illness include fever and appearing toxic with unstable comorbidities.
Surgical consultation and management are needed for I&D of a large or deep-seated abscess.
Guideline-based care improves appropriateness of prescribing for patients with cellulitis and skin abscess.

A 6-month multicenter retrospective study of purulent SSTIs in the elderly found that, despite adherence to the 2014 IDSA guidelines, treatment failure following visits at the emergency department was high among patients 65 years and older (OR 3.9, 95% CI 1.2-12.1). For every 10 years of incremental age increase, the odds of failing initial treatment increased by 43% (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1-1.9).
Tetracyclines and quinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Tetracyclines are contraindicated in those eight years and younger.
Quinolones are contraindicated in children.
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) is the best empirical therapeutic choice (TMP dose of 10 mg/kg/day in 2 doses; not to exceed adult dose).
Clindamycin is also an option (10-20 mg/kg/day in 3-4 doses; not to exceed adult dose).

A randomized trial compared clindamycin with cephalexin for children with an uncomplicated superficial skin abscess; 70% had MRSA. All underwent incision and drainage. Fully 95% improved at 2 to 3 days, regardless of the antibiotic, and despite the fact that cephalexin is not active against MRSA, confirming the primacy of I&D as the primary therapy. Another study randomized 161 children ages 3 months to 18 years with skin abscess requiring drainage to TMP/SMX or placebo for 10 days. Clinical failure rates were similar at 10 days.

cell.label: Patient presents with "spider bite," pustular lesions, "boils" abscess (with tissue necrosis), cellulitis, impetigo, or infected wound.

Incise and drain abscess; if not performed, consider culture of draining wound, or aspirate or biopsy of central area of inflammation. Obtain culture and sensitivities (include "D-test" for clindamycin resistance if MRSA). Educate patient regarding infection control and wound care. Assess severity.

Outpatient management: Local care, I&D, ± topical antibiotics may be sufficient; oral antibiotics effective; beta-lactam antibiotics preferred for MSSA; if increased suspicion for MRSA based on presence of ≥1 risk factors, consider empiric therapy active against MRSA; adjust antibiotics based on results of culture & susceptibility testing; monitor response to therapy.
Febrile, appears ill, but no unstable comorbidities.

Outpatient management: Low suspicion for MRSA; beta-lactam antibiotics preferred for MSSA; if increased suspicion for MRSA based on presence of ≥1 risk factors, consider empiric therapy active against MRSA; adjust antibiotics based on results of culture & susceptibility testing; monitor response to therapy.
Appears toxic, unstable comorbidity, or limb-threatening infection; sepsis syndrome or life-threatening infection (e.g., necrotizing fasciitis).

Hospital management: Empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics including vancomycin for activity against S. aureus & MRSA; adjust therapy based on results of culture & susceptibility testing; monitor response to therapy; consult infectious disease specialist if no improvement or consider alternative agents (e.g., linezolid, daptomycin); switch to oral therapy based on susceptibility testing if: afebrile for 24 hours, clinically improved, able to take oral therapy, and close follow-up is possible.

feature.feature_body: History of previous MRSA infection or colonization Any of following within past 12 months: hospitalization; dialysis or renal failure, diabetes; surgery; long-term care residence; indwelling catheter or medical device History of injection drug use or incarceration Close contact with someone known to be infected or colonized with MRSA High prevalence of MRSA in community or population Data from Stevens DL, Bisno AL, Chambers HF, et al.
